description: Rounding each purchase up to the next whole number and saving the difference turns spare change into a steady habit.

body.heading: How it works
paragraphs: Buy something for $3.40 and you move 60 cents to savings, rounding the spend up to $4. A $12.25 purchase contributes 75 cents. Some banking apps do this automatically; a notebook and a weekly transfer do it manually.

Individually the amounts are trivial. Across twenty purchases a week, though, an average round-up of about 50 cents each becomes roughly $10 a week — over $500 a year — collected from money you barely noticed spending.

body.heading: Why painless works
paragraphs: Saving systems fail when they hurt. Round-ups succeed because the sacrifice sits below the threshold of regret: nobody's week is ruined by 60 cents. The habit survives busy months, tired months, and expensive months alike.
That durability is the whole point. A modest system you keep for a year beats a heroic system you abandon in February.

body.heading: Give the pot a purpose
paragraphs: Round-ups grow faster with a destination: a treats fund, a gifts pot, a first emergency cushion. Check the pot monthly, enjoy watching it climb, and let it do its named job when the time comes.

If your bank does not offer automatic round-ups, a manual version works: once a week, move the odd amount that takes your current account to a round number. It takes thirty seconds and keeps the same painless spirit.

takeaway: Round every purchase up and save the change: pennies per purchase, hundreds per year, and a habit too painless to quit.
